quote_verbatim: The outstanding item of importance in my selection of partners, as well as in my subsequent relations with them, has been the determination that we use the same yardstick.
concept: Yardstick - shared standard between manager and partners
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 (discount-rate genealogy); Owner's Manual principle 1 (partnership attitude)
evolution_notes: Origin of the yardstick concept: a pre-agreed PERFORMANCE standard, not a discount rate. Evolves: Dow par (E1) -> government-bond yardstick (1994/1997 meetings) -> S&P 500 (OM-15).

quote_verbatim: I believe in establishing yardsticks prior to the act; retrospectively, almost anything can be made to look good in relation to something or other.
concept: Pre-commitment to measurement standards
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 (define thesis-confirming/breaking metrics BEFORE entry); Workbook Sheet 6/9
evolution_notes: Primary-source ancestor of the framework's before-entry metric commitment - 60 years before the May 2026 edition asserted it without citation.

quote_verbatim: I have continuously used the Dow-Jones Industrial Average as our measure of par. It is my feeling that three years is a very minimal test of performance, and the best test consists of a period at least that long where the terminal level of the Dow is reasonably close to the initial level.
concept: Benchmark discipline; minimum measurement horizon
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 monitoring; OM-15 mapping (S&P yardstick)
evolution_notes: Three-year minimum test contrasts with the framework's two-consecutive-quarters exit rule - the corpus supports patience horizons, conventions must own the quarterly cadence.

quote_verbatim: A lot of value can be obtained for the price paid. This substantial excess of value creates a comfortable margin of safety in each transaction. This individual margin of safety, coupled with a diversity of commitments creates a most attractive package of safety and appreciation potential.
concept: Margin of safety - earliest articulation in Buffett's own words
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 Step 5 (MOS)
evolution_notes: E1 MOS = per-transaction excess value PLUS diversity of commitments (quantitative-era). Evolves to concentrated wonderful-business MOS: 1989 letter, 1992 letter ('cornerstone').

quote_verbatim: You will not be right simply because a large number of people momentarily agree with you. You will not be right simply because important people agree with you. [...] You will be right, over the course of many transactions, if your hypotheses are correct, your facts are correct, and your reasoning is correct. True conservatism is only possible through knowledge and reason.
concept: Independent reasoning as the only real conservatism
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 1 (independent verification); Gate 5 (inversion's epistemic basis)
evolution_notes: Restated 1962 letter; reformulated 1964 letter (E1-06). The framework's 'independent verification without management's narrative' rule descends from this.

quote_verbatim: Truly conservative actions arise from intelligent hypotheses, correct facts and sound reasoning. [...] We derive no comfort because important people, vocal people, or great numbers of people agree with us. Nor do we derive comfort if they don't. A public opinion poll is no substitute for thought.
concept: Anti-consensus epistemics
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 1; Gate 5
evolution_notes: Matured restatement of E1-05.

quote_verbatim: When we really sit back with a smile on our face is when we run into a situation we can understand, where the facts are ascertainable and clear, and the course of action obvious.
concept: Understanding as precondition - circle of competence precursor
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 1 (Circle of Competence)
evolution_notes: The circle-of-competence CONCEPT is fully present in 1964; the PHRASE arrives in the 1996 BRK letter (claims_audit C12). v3.0 should footnote this development.

quote_verbatim: 7. We diversify substantially less than most investment operations. We might invest up to 40% of our net worth in a single security under conditions coupling an extremely high probability that our facts and reasoning are correct with a very low probability that anything could drastically change the underlying value of the investment.
concept: Concentration - the 40% ground rule
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 (position sizing)
evolution_notes: Earliest concentration policy. Evolves to 1993 letter concentration-decreases-risk (verified, claims_audit C09) and Munger Talk 2 'the wise ones bet heavily'.

quote_verbatim: Frankly, there is nothing I would like better than to have 50 different investment opportunities, all of which have a mathematical expectation (this term reflects the range of all possible relative performances, including negative ones, adjusted for the probability of each - no yawning, please) of achieving performance surpassing the Dow by, say, fifteen percentage points per annum.
concept: Expected-value framing of position selection
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7; Gate 8 (asymmetry ratio's honest ancestor)
evolution_notes: THE corpus basis for probabilistic sizing - replaces the unattested Kelly Criterion attribution (claims_audit C28) together with Munger Talk 2 bet-heavily passage. REPAIRED 2026-09-20, operator-authorised (decision 12): the cell had substituted an editorial bracket, '[performance superior to the Dow]', for the letter's own 'performance surpassing the Dow by, say, fifteen percentage points per annum', which dropped the magnitude - the interesting half of the sentence. The letter's words are restored, the row now inserts no text of its own, and the quote is one continuous sentence of the 1966-01-20 letter, so it carries no elision.

quote_verbatim: We are obviously only going to go to 40% in very rare situations - this rarity, of course, is what makes it necessary that we concentrate so heavily, when we see such an opportunity. [...] They are also going to have to possess such superior qualitative and/or quantitative factors that the chance of serious permanent loss is minimal (anything can happen on a short-term quotational basis which partially explains the greater risk of widened year-to-year variation in results).
concept: Risk = permanent loss, not quotational variation
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 (MOS rationale); Gate 7 (sizing); Glossary risk definition
evolution_notes: Permanent-loss-vs-quotation distinction later formalized in 1993 letter ('possibility of loss or injury').

quote_verbatim: 6. I am not in the business of predicting general stock market or business fluctuations. If you think I can do this, or think it is essential to an investment program, you should not be in the partnership.
concept: No market forecasting
supports_gate_or_sheet: Introduction (what the framework is not); Gate 8 framing
evolution_notes: Constant across all eras; cf. 1994 meeting (no macro inputs) and OM-13's rationale for reticence.

quote_verbatim: a. Our investments will be chosen on the basis of value, not popularity;
concept: Value not popularity
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6; Mr. Market genealogy
evolution_notes: Buffett's own pre-Berkshire statement of the value discipline he learned from Graham - cite this, not Graham directly (shelf amendment 2026-07-13).

quote_verbatim: A work-out is an investment which is dependent on a specific corporate action for its profit rather than a general advance in the price of the stock as in the case of undervalued situations. Work-outs come about through: sales, mergers, liquidations, tenders, etc.
concept: Category taxonomy: generals / work-outs (later + controls)
supports_gate_or_sheet: Historical context for Gate 2's segment thinking; not gate-mapped
evolution_notes: Shows the method BEFORE the quality evolution; v3.0 history section material.

quote_verbatim: Figured very roughly, the $30,000 invested at 4% compounded annually would have amounted to something like $2,000,000,000,000 (that's $2 trillion for those of you who are not government statisticians) by 1962. [...] Such fanciful geometric progressions illustrate the value of either living a long time, or compounding your money at a decent rate.
concept: Compounding as the central force
supports_gate_or_sheet: Abstract / central claim (time as compounding force)
evolution_notes: The framework's central claim cites (Buffett, 1989); this is the 27-years-earlier articulation. Ellipsis spans the Manhattan-Indians sentence.

quote_verbatim: Interestingly enough, although I consider myself to be primarily in the quantitative school [...] the really sensational ideas I have had over the years have been heavily weighted toward the qualitative side where I have had a "high-probability insight". This is what causes the cash register to really sing. However, it is an infrequent occurrence, as insights usually are, and, of course, no insight is required on the quantitative side - the figures should hit you over the head with a baseball bat. So the really big money tends to be made by investors who are right on qualitative decisions but, at least in my opinion, the more sure money tends to be made on the obvious quantitative decisions.
concept: The quantitative-to-qualitative pivot
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gates 1-2 (why quality precedes valuation); framework sequence rationale
evolution_notes: THE documented pivot from Graham-style statistical bargains toward quality - predates Munger-influence narrative usually dated to See's (1972) and the 1989 letter's 'wonderful company' line. Also: 'Such statistical bargains have tended to disappear over the years.' (same letter).

quote_verbatim: The primary test of managerial economic performance is the achievement of a high earnings rate on equity capital employed (without undue leverage, accounting gimmickry, etc.) and not the achievement of consistent gains in earnings per share.
concept: Return on equity capital as THE performance test
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 4 (financial quality); Gate 3 Dimension 2 (competence)
evolution_notes: The corpus-native basis for return-on-capital tests; the framework's ROIC>15%/25% thresholds remain conventions, but the TEST itself is 1979 Buffett.

quote_verbatim: And, if conditions persist - if all earnings are paid out and return on equity stays at 14% - the 7% tax-exempt equivalent to the higher-bracket individual investor is just as frozen as is the coupon on a tax-exempt bond. [...] If, on the other hand, all earnings of our typical American business are retained and return on equity again remains constant, earnings will grow at 14% per year.
concept: Equity as a bond with a coupon set by return on equity
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6-B field amendment (growing-coupon reading of the yardstick)
evolution_notes: The equity-as-disguised-bond passage the Jul-2026 field amendment asked to find. Companion to the 1977 Fortune essay (off disk); 1997 meeting Q12 questioner cites that essay's 12%-par framing. REPAIRED 2026-09-20, operator-authorised (decision 12): the cell previously printed the RETENTION sentence first and the frozen-coupon conclusion second with the words 'if all earnings are' cut off its front, so read as written the frozen coupon attached to the retention case. THE LETTER SAYS THE OPPOSITE: the frozen 7% tax-exempt equivalent is the PAID-OUT case ('if all earnings are paid out and return on equity stays at 14%'), and the retained case 'will grow at 14% per year'. Buffett's point in that passage is that the two cases differ. Both fragments now stand in the letter's own order with the front of the first restored.

quote_verbatim: An individual, stuck with a 5% bond with many years to run before maturity, does not take the coupons from that bond and pay one hundred cents on the dollar for more 5% bonds while similar bonds are available at, say, forty cents on the dollar. [...] What makes sense for the bondholder makes sense for the shareholder.
concept: Bondholder logic applied to equity capital allocation
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 3 Dimension 2 (retention/reinvestment tests); OM-9 mapping
evolution_notes: Grounds the retained-earnings test: reinvest only where returns beat alternatives.

quote_verbatim: businesses logically are worth far more than net tangible assets when they can be expected to produce earnings on such assets considerably in excess of market rates of return. The capitalized value of this excess return is economic Goodwill.
year: 1983 (appendix: Goodwill and its Amortization: The Rules and The Realities)
concept: Economic goodwill defined
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 2 (intangible-asset moat basis)
evolution_notes: Corrects claims_audit C04: source is the 1983 appendix, not the 1987 letter. Same appendix: See's 'earning about $2 million on $8 million of net tangible assets' - i.e., 25% after tax on net tangible assets - the honest ancestor of the misattributed '25% on equity' Munger-Wesco quote (C21).

quote_verbatim: It is possible, of course, that See's economic Goodwill will disappear. But it won't shrink in even decrements or anything remotely resembling them. What is more likely is that the Goodwill will increase - in current, if not in constant, dollars - because of inflation. That probability exists because true economic Goodwill tends to rise in nominal value proportionally with inflation.
concept: Economic goodwill compounds nominally with inflation
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 2 (why intangible moats endure without capital)
evolution_notes: The framework's 'does not depreciate with time' gloss traces here (and to the 1999 letter's 'much like land' restatement, E4).

quote_verbatim: When companies with outstanding businesses and comfortable financial positions find their shares selling far below intrinsic value in the marketplace, no alternative action can benefit shareholders as surely as repurchases.
concept: Buybacks below intrinsic value
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 3 Dimension 2 (say no to buybacks at bad prices - and yes at good ones)
evolution_notes: Price/value-conditional endorsement; same passage condemns greenmail. Evolves: 2011 letter buyback policy (E5).

quote_verbatim: we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful.
concept: Contrarian temperament
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 behavioral rule; Introduction
evolution_notes: Note the asymmetry usually lost in quotation: greedy ONLY when others are fearful.

quote_verbatim: we can gain some insights about what may be called "owner earnings." These represent (a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges such as Company N's items (1) and (4) less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment, etc. that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume. (If the business requires additional working capital to maintain its competitive position and unit volume, the increment also should be included in (c). However, businesses following the LIFO inventory method usually do not require additional working capital if unit volume does not change.)
concept: Owner earnings - the complete definition INCLUDING working capital
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 4; Workbook Sheet 5 (which correctly includes WC); corrects Framework/42P formula (claims_audit C01)
evolution_notes: 1997 meeting Q14 confirms practitioners read (c) as 'maintenance capital spending and working capital requirements'. The framework's Net Income + D&A - MaintCapEx omits the WC clause. ALIAS NOTE (2026-09-20, decision 20): one passage, two ids. This row is the LONGER cut of the 1986 owner-earnings definition and [E2-23] is the same passage without its opening clause. The 132 runs of record cite E2-23 117 times and this row zero times. Both ids resolve and neither is retired; Curriculum/CHARTER.md was repointed from E2-08 to E2-23 on 2026-09-20.

quote_verbatim: Our owner-earnings equation does not yield the deceptively precise figures provided by GAAP, since (c) must be a guess - and one sometimes very difficult to make. Despite this problem, we consider the owner earnings figure, not the GAAP figure, to be the relevant item for valuation purposes [...] We agree with Keynes's observation: "I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong."
concept: Owner earnings is an estimate; precision is false
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 4; Gate 6 Step 6 (sensitivity); glossary
evolution_notes: Buffett attributes the approximately-right idea to Keynes here; his own 1993 restatement ('It is better to be approximately right than precisely wrong') is E3. Fixes the 'Buffett, multiple letters' hand-wave (C30).

quote_verbatim: The difference between GEICO's costs and those of its competitors is a kind of moat that protects a valuable and much-sought-after business castle. No one understands this moat-around-the-castle concept better than Bill Snyder, Chairman of GEICO. He continually widens the moat by driving down costs still more, thereby defending and strengthening the economic franchise.
concept: First 'moat' usage - cost-advantage moat, widening as management's job
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 2 (moat identification; cost-advantage type; WIDENING direction)
evolution_notes: Confirms C03. Note: the first moat named in the letters is a COST-ADVANTAGE moat, measured by expense ratio vs competitors - the framework's cost-moat metric ('gross margin vs competitors') has this as its ancestor. 'Economic franchise' appears here too, before the 1991 franchise/business taxonomy (E3).

quote_verbatim: the investment income that an insurer earns from holding on to policyholders' funds ("the float")
concept: Float - first compact definition in the letters
supports_gate_or_sheet: Context for OM-7 mapping; sidebar material
evolution_notes: Canonical full definition arrives in the 1990s letters and OM-7 ('the funds of others that our insurance business holds because it receives premiums before needing to pay out losses').

quote_verbatim: Ben Graham, my friend and teacher, long ago described the mental attitude toward market fluctuations that I believe to be most conducive to investment success. He said that you should imagine market quotations as coming from a remarkably accommodating fellow named Mr. Market who is your partner in a private business. Without fail, Mr. Market appears daily and names a price at which he will either buy your interest or sell you his. [...] the poor fellow has incurable emotional problems.
concept: Mr. Market - Buffett's own retelling
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6/8 (price vs value); Introduction
evolution_notes: Per shelf amendment 2026-07-13: this is how Graham enters v3.0 - named inside Buffett's quote, not cited independently. Continues: 'It may give us the chance to buy more of a good thing at a bargain price.'

quote_verbatim: Following Ben's teachings, Charlie and I let our marketable equities tell us by their operating results - not by their daily, or even yearly, price quotations - whether our investments are successful. The market may ignore business success for a while, but eventually will confirm it. As Ben said: "In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run it is a weighing machine."
concept: Operating results, not quotations, as the verdict
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 monitoring (metric-driven, not price-driven)
evolution_notes: Direct primary basis for the framework's never-sell-on-price-alone rule.

quote_verbatim: when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever. We are just the opposite of those who hurry to sell and book profits when companies perform well but who tenaciously hang on to businesses that disappoint.
concept: Favorite holding period is forever - conditional on quality
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 sell discipline
evolution_notes: Note the CONDITION (outstanding business + outstanding management) - forever is earned, not automatic. Peter Lynch flowers/weeds simile follows in the same passage.

quote_verbatim: If you buy a stock at a sufficiently low price, there will usually be some hiccup in the fortunes of the business that gives you a chance to unload at a decent profit, even though the long-term performance of the business may be terrible. I call this the "cigar butt" approach to investing. A cigar butt found on the street that has only one puff left in it may not offer much of a smoke, but the "bargain purchase" will make that puff all profit. Unless you are a liquidator, that kind of approach to buying businesses is foolish.
concept: Cigar-butt investing rejected
supports_gate_or_sheet: Introduction (evolution narrative); Gate 2 rationale
evolution_notes: Completes the E1-15 evolution arc: 1967 'statistical bargains have tended to disappear' -> 1989 explicit rejection.

quote_verbatim: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner. But now, when buying companies or common stocks, we look for first-class businesses accompanied by first-class managements.
concept: Wonderful at fair beats fair at wonderful - Buffett crediting Munger
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 (Statute Book One: wonderful-at-fair); corrects Gate 6 epigraph misattribution (C16)
evolution_notes: Buffett's sentence, Munger's influence acknowledged in the next clause - v3.0 should quote both sentences together.

quote_verbatim: I've said many times that when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact.
concept: Business economics beat managerial brilliance
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 2 before Gate 3 (sequence rationale)
evolution_notes: Adjacent: 'Good jockeys will do well on good horses, but not on broken-down nags.'

quote_verbatim: My most surprising discovery: the overwhelming importance in business of an unseen force that we might call "the institutional imperative." [...] I thought then that decent, intelligent, and experienced managers would automatically make rational business decisions. But I learned over time that isn't so. Instead, rationality frequently wilts when the institutional imperative comes into play.
concept: The institutional imperative
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 3 (management evaluation); Gate 5 (management-failure inversion)
evolution_notes: Confirms C40 origin. The 1990 letter restates the definition ('the tendency of executives to mindlessly imitate the behavior of their peers') - E3.

quote_verbatim: Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre.
concept: Time compounds quality and erodes mediocrity
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 2 classification rationale; Abstract central claim
evolution_notes: Verified verbatim (C06). The specific fade-year structures built on it remain FRAMEWORK CONVENTIONS.

quote_verbatim: It is in the nature of things, as Jacobi knew, that many hard problems are best solved only when they are addressed backward.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 01 - Harvard School Commencement Speech (1986-06-13).txt
concept: Inversion - Jacobi
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 5; Gate 8
evolution_notes: Corrects C26: Talk 1 (1986), not USC 1994. The talk demonstrates inversion via 'prescriptions for misery'.

quote_verbatim: Darwin's result was due in large measure to his working method, which violated all my rules for misery and particularly emphasized a backward twist in that he always gave priority attention to evidence tending to disconfirm whatever cherished and hard-won theory he already had.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 01 - Harvard School Commencement Speech (1986-06-13).txt
concept: Disconfirming evidence - the Darwin method
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 5 (Step B: construct the failure scenario)
evolution_notes: Replaces the Fitzgerald-conflated quote (C27 item 5).

quote_verbatim: Lethargy bordering on sloth remains the cornerstone of our investment style: This year we neither bought nor sold a share of five of our six major holdings.
concept: Inactivity as explicit style
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7 Final Rule
evolution_notes: Precedes the 1996 'Inactivity strikes us as intelligent behavior' (E3-15/C13). Letter recovered in full 2026-07-13.

quote_verbatim: Most have resulted from a managerial failing that we described last year when discussing the "institutional imperative:" the tendency of executives to mindlessly imitate the behavior of their peers, no matter how foolish it may be to do so.
concept: Institutional imperative - compact definition
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 3; Gate 5 (management-failure inversion)
evolution_notes: Restates the 1989 origin (E2-18) in one sentence.

quote_verbatim: An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation. The existence of all three conditions will be demonstrated by a company's ability to regularly price its product or service aggressively and thereby to earn high rates of return on capital. Moreover, franchises can tolerate mis-management.
concept: Franchise vs business - Buffett's own moat taxonomy
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 2 (the corpus-native alternative to the Dorsey four-type taxonomy)
evolution_notes: THE Buffett moat test: pricing power demonstrated in returns on capital. v3.0 Gate 2 should lead with this; the four-type taxonomy stays as a labeled convention. 'Weak franchises or strong businesses' = the middle ground.

quote_verbatim: look-through earnings, which consist of: (1) the operating earnings reported in the previous section, plus; (2) the retained operating earnings of major investees that, under GAAP accounting, are not reflected in our profits, less; (3) an allowance for the tax that would be paid by Berkshire if these retained earnings of investees had instead been distributed to us.
concept: Look-through earnings - full definition
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 4 (partial-ownership analog of owner earnings); OM-6 mapping
evolution_notes: Fills the gap flagged in owners_manual_map (OM-6): the concept was absent from the May framework.

quote_verbatim: Leaving the question of price aside, the best business to own is one that over an extended period can employ large amounts of incremental capital at very high rates of return. The worst business to own is one that must, or will, do the opposite - that is, consistently employ ever-greater amounts of capital at very low rates of return.
concept: Incremental returns define business quality
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 4 (return on incremental capital test)
evolution_notes: Buffett's own statement of the ROIC-primacy idea the framework misattributed to Munger/Wesco (C21/C22). Pair with Munger Talk 2 6%/18% (E3-17).

quote_verbatim: the two approaches are joined at the hip: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value, constituting a variable whose importance can range from negligible to enormous and whose impact can be negative as well as positive. In addition, we think the very term "value investing" is redundant. What is "investing" if it is not the act of seeking value at least sufficient to justify the amount paid?
concept: Value vs growth is a false dichotomy
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 (growth scenarios belong INSIDE the value calculation)
evolution_notes: Munger's 2000-meeting 'all intelligent investing is value investing' (E4) is the companion quote.

quote_verbatim: In The Theory of Investment Value, written over 50 years ago, John Burr Williams set forth the equation for value [...] the investment analyst must himself estimate the future "coupons." [...] The investment shown by the discounted-flows-of-cash calculation to be the cheapest is the one that the investor should purchase - irrespective of whether the business grows or doesn't, displays volatility or smoothness in its earnings, or carries a high price or low in relation to its current earnings and book value.
concept: DCF as the value equation; equities as bonds with self-estimated coupons
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 (the DCF's true corpus foundation); Gate 6-B (growing-coupon reading)
evolution_notes: Buffett's own DCF authority - replaces the Graham-1949 citation (shelf amendment). 'Estimate the future coupons' extends the 1981 frozen-coupon passage (E2-02).

quote_verbatim: At Berkshire, we attempt to deal with this problem in two ways. First, we try to stick to businesses we believe we understand. That means they must be relatively simple and stable in character. If a business is complex or subject to constant change, we're not smart enough to predict future cash flows. [...] Second, and equally important, we insist on a margin of safety in our purchase price. If we calculate the value of a common stock to be only slightly higher than its price, we're not interested in buying. We believe this margin-of-safety principle, so strongly emphasized by Ben Graham, to be the cornerstone of investment success.
concept: the TWO defences, in Buffett's own order: understanding FIRST, margin of safety second
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 Step 5
evolution_notes: RE-CUT 2026-08-26. The row previously carried only the second half, which inverted Buffett's own ordering - he names understanding first and says of the margin of safety only 'Second, and equally important'. Quoting the MOS alone made it look like the primary defence. The first half is rowed separately and in full at E3-31. TEXT NOTE: source file is hard-wrapped at ~60 chars; line breaks removed to reassemble the sentences. No other change. Graham named inside Buffett's sentence per the shelf amendment. The specific 20%/30% MOS thresholds were framework inventions and are retired in v4.

quote_verbatim: we define risk, using dictionary terms, as "the possibility of loss or injury." Academics, however, like to define investment "risk" differently, averring that it is the relative volatility of a stock or portfolio of stocks [...]
concept: Risk = possibility of loss, not volatility/beta
supports_gate_or_sheet: Glossary; Gate 6 (MOS rationale); Gate 7
evolution_notes: Formalizes E1-10 (permanent loss vs quotational variation, 1965).

quote_verbatim: The primary factors bearing upon this evaluation are: 1) The certainty with which the long-term economic characteristics of the business can be evaluated; 2) The certainty with which management can be evaluated, both as to its ability to realize the full potential of the business and to wisely employ its cash flows; 3) The certainty with which management can be counted on to channel the rewards from the business to the shareholders rather than to itself; 4) The purchase price of the business; 5) The levels of taxation and inflation that will be experienced [...]
concept: Buffett's five risk factors
supports_gate_or_sheet: THE GATE SEQUENCE ITSELF: factors 1-3 = Gates 1-3, factor 4 = Gate 6, factor 5 = context
evolution_notes: The strongest structural authority in the corpus for a sequential, quality-before-price framework. The May edition never cites it.

quote_verbatim: We believe that a policy of portfolio concentration may well decrease risk if it raises, as it should, both the intensity with which an investor thinks about a business and the comfort-level he must feel with its economic characteristics before buying into it.
concept: Concentration decreases risk (conditionally)
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 7
evolution_notes: Verified (C09). Completes E1-08/E1-09 arc.

quote_verbatim: In their hunger for a single statistic to measure risk, however, they forget a fundamental principle: It is better to be approximately right than precisely wrong.
concept: Approximately right beats precisely wrong
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6 Step 6 (sensitivity grid); Scream Test rationale
evolution_notes: Buffett's restatement of Keynes (see E2-09). Fixes C30's vague 'multiple letters'.

quote_verbatim: Well, I would say that in a world of 7 percent long-term bond rates that we would certainly want to think we were discounting future after-tax streams of cash at at least a 10 percent rate. But that will depend on the certainty we feel about the business. The more certain we feel about a business, the closer we are willing to play it. We have to feel pretty certain about any business before we’re even interested at all. But there are still degrees of certainty, and — If we thought we were getting a stream of cash over the next 30 years that we felt extremely certain about, we would use a discount rate that would be somewhat less than if it was one where we thought we might get some surprises in five or 10 years — possibility existed.
concept: The 1994 'at least 10%' - the SAME quit point as 2002/2003, NOT a +3 spread; and certainty moves the rate DOWN toward the bond, not up from a floor
supports_gate_or_sheet: Gate 6-B (Statute); replaces the fabricated 'That's my yardstick' quote (C10)
evolution_notes: RE-CUT 2026-08-28 (Test D). The prior cut ended before the final sentence, and the row was read as 'a +3% certainty spread over the long bond (10 minus 7), widened for less certainty' - the interpretation the 2002 letter's second data point (10% at a ~5% bond) falsifies and 1996:623-625 [E3-42] calls 'mathematical gibberish'. You either get into a different business or you’re dead—you’re destroyed. It happens again and again and again. And when these new businesses come in, there are huge advantages for the early birds. quote_verbatim: In most businesses, of course, insolvent companies run out of cash. Insurance is different: you can be broke but flush. In fact, these “walking dead” often redouble their efforts to write business, accepting almost any price or risk, simply to keep the cash flowing in. With an attitude like that of an embezzler who has gambled away his purloined funds, these companies hope that somehow they can get lucky on the next batch of business and thereby cover up earlier shortfalls. Even if they don’t get lucky, the penalty to managers is usually no greater for a $100 million shortfall than one of $10 million; in the meantime, while the losses mount, the managers keep their jobs and perquisites.

concept: GOOD BUSINESS vs GOOD INVESTMENT - business quality is defined by capital NEEDED IN the business; investment quality by the price paid; the two judgments never merge
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q2/Q5 boundary (why the sequence exists); Q4
evolution_notes: Register M2-24. 2010 meeting line 1097 ('you could run the Coca-Cola Company, assuming you had the bottling systems, with no capital'); negative-capital classes named (magazines, Blue Chip Stamps float). 2020:1683-95 verified as companion: 'they don't take much capital. And that's why they're worth a lot of money.' This is why Q2-Q4 judge the business and only Q5 judges the price - ASML 2026-08-28 is the worked case: a great business refused as an investment.

quote_verbatim: we don’t have any formula that evaluates risk, but we certainly make our own calculation of risk versus reward in every transaction we do. And that’s true whether it’s marketable securities, that’s true whether it’s private investments, that’s true whether it’s making an investment in a business. And sometimes we’re wrong, and we’re going to be wrong sometimes in the future. You can’t make a lot of decisions in this business without being wrong. But we don’t think the procedure — or the results — would be changed favorably by having lots of committees and lots of spreadsheets and that sort of thing. It just — you know — If I had a group under me, they would try and figure out what I wanted the answer to be, and they would tell me what I wanted to hear. And I’ve watched that approach at 20 public companies.
concept: FORMULAS RETURN DESIRED ANSWERS - 'If I had a group under me, they would try and figure out what I wanted the answer to be'; no committees, no spreadsheet apparatus
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q5 (the ONE BOOK's reason: engines compute, never vote); E3-24 scope
evolution_notes: Register M2-28. 2019 meeting lines 1147-1153; line 1153: 'if the hurdle rate is 15 percent or something, having them all come out at 15.1 or 15.2, because that's what's going to happen.' Scope on E3-24: the quantified death mechanism stays - line 1149 does the math itself ('we go on to figure out the math of gain versus loss and how much loss we can afford') - but it is the analyst's own arithmetic AFTER the understanding hurdle, never an apparatus that manufactures the wanted output. The DCF-as-engine-not-vote rule carries this as its reason.

quote_verbatim: In some businesses, the participants behave like a demented Kellogg. In other businesses, they don’t. Unfortunately, I do not have a perfect model for predicting how that’s going to happen. For example, if you look around at bottler markets, you’ll find many markets where bottlers of Pepsi and Coke both make a lot of money and many others where they destroy most of the profitability of the two franchises. That must get down to the peculiarities of individual adjustment to market capitalism. I think you’d have to know the people involved to fully understand what was happening.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 02 - A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom (USC, 1994-04-14).txt
concept: THE PEOPLE RESIDUAL - identical structures produce different profits ('a demented Kellogg'); 'I do not have a perfect model for predicting how that's going to happen'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q2 (the competitor row's stated limit); Q3

I think you'd have to know the people involved.' The causal model [E4-36] carries a residual no structural analysis reaches; the competitor row shows position, not conduct.

quote_verbatim: there are all kinds of wonderful new inventions that give you nothing as owners except the opportunity to spend a lot more money in a business that’s still going to be lousy. The money still won’t come to you. All of the advantages from great improvements are going to flow through to the customers. Conversely, if you own the only newspaper in Oshkosh and they were to invent more efficient ways of composing the whole newspaper, then when you got rid of the old technology and got new, fancy computers and so forth, all of the savings would come right through to the bottom line. In all cases, the people who sell the machinery—and, by and large, even the internal bureaucrats urging you to buy the equipment—show you projections with the amount you’ll save at current prices with the new technology. However, they don’t do the second step of the analysis, which is to determine how much is going to stay home and how much is just going to flow through to the customer. I’ve never seen a single projection incorporating that second step in my life.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 02 - A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom (USC, 1994-04-14).txt
concept: THE SECOND STEP - who KEEPS the productivity gains: in a commodity business they flow to customers; in the Oshkosh monopoly they stick; no vendor projection ever asks
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q2 (capex evaluation by moat class); Q3 flags (vendor projections); Q4 (c)
evolution_notes: Register P-21. Talk 02:231-235, the textile-loom lesson worked ('Nothing was going to stick to our ribs as owners'). I've never seen a single projection incorporating that second step.' The commodity equation [E2-58] from the capex side; E3-48's nine-in-ten projections lack exactly this step.

quote_verbatim: So you do get an occasional opportunity to get into a wonderful business that’s being run by a wonderful manager. And, of course, that’s hog heaven day. If you don’t load up when you get those opportunities, it’s a big mistake. Occasionally, you’ll find a human being who’s so talented that he can do things that ordinary skilled mortals can’t. I would argue that —who was second-generation in Marks and Spencer of England—was such a man. Patterson was such a man at National Cash Register. And Sam Walton was such a man. These people do come along, and, in many cases, they’re not all that hard to identify.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 02 - A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom (USC, 1994-04-14).txt
concept: LOAD UP ON HOG-HEAVEN DAYS - wonderful business + wonderful manager: 'If you don't load up when you get those opportunities, it's a big mistake'; the superstars 'in many cases... not all that hard to identify'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q5 sizing (E3-45's companion); Q3 (the E2-48 class, identifiable)

quote_verbatim: Another very simple effect I very seldom see discussed either by investment managers or anybody else is the effect of taxes. If you’re going to buy something that compounds for 30 years at 15 percent per annum and you pay one 35 percent tax at the very end, the way that works out is that after taxes, you keep 13.3 percent per annum. In contrast, if you bought the same investment but had to pay taxes every year of 35 percent out of the 15 percent that you earned, then your return would be 15 percent minus 35 percent of 15 percent—or only 9.75 percent per year compounded. So the difference there is over 3.5 percent. And what 3.5 percent does to the numbers over long holding periods like 30 years is truly eye-opening. If you sit on your ass for long, long stretches in great companies, you can get a huge edge from nothing but the way income taxes work.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 02 - A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom (USC, 1994-04-14).txt
concept: THE TAX-DEFERRAL EDGE QUANTIFIED - 15%/30yr taxed once at the end keeps 13.3%/yr vs 9.75% taxed annually: over 3.5 points from sitting still - WITH its counterweight: over-minimizing taxes is a standard dumb mistake
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q6 (binds trigger 2 with E2-46); Q5 ranking
evolution_notes: Register P-25. Talk 02:401-413; the counterweight at 407: 'trying to minimize taxes too much is one of the great standard causes of really dumb mistakes. I see terrible mistakes from people being overly motivated by tax considerations.' Both directions bind: the switch must clear the deferral penalty [E2-46], AND tax must never veto a right decision - the corpus's own 2024 Apple trim and the ASML 2026-08-28 exit both paid the tax when the view crystallized [E2-40].

quote_verbatim: we bought it at about 20 percent of the value to a private owner. So we bought it on a Ben Graham-style basis—at one-fifth of obvious value—and, in addition, we faced a situation where you had both the top hand in a game that was clearly going to end up with one winner and a management with a lot of integrity and intelligence. That one was a real dream. They’re very high-class people, the Katharine Graham family. That’s why it was a dream—an absolute, damn dream.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 02 - A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom (USC, 1994-04-14).txt

quote_verbatim: the culture and legal systems of the United States are especially favorable to shareholder interests compared to other interests and compared to most other countries. Indeed, there are many other countries where any good going to public shareholders has a very low priority and almost every other constituency stands higher in line. This factor, I think, is under-weighed at many investment institutions, probably because it does not easily lead to quantitative thinking using modern financial technique. But some important factor doesn’t lose share of force just because some “expert” can better measure other types of force.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 06 - Investment Practices of Leading Charitable Foundations (1998-10-14).txt

This full cost doesn’t show up in conventional accounting. But that is because accounting has limitations and not because the full cost isn’t present.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 06 - Investment Practices of Leading Charitable Foundations (1998-10-14).txt
concept: THE CROUPIERS' TAKE - management plus frictional costs of getting in and out 'can easily reach 3 percent per annum'; invisible to accounting, inescapable in aggregate
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q6 (a switch's gross spread must clear friction too); Q5

Talk 07:71-77 companion not re-read this pass. With E2-46 (tax) and E4-45 (threshold): the full switching bar is tax + friction + a material gap.

quote_verbatim: His formal education is wide enough to cover practically everything useful in piloting. His knowledge of practically everything needed by pilots is not taught just well enough to enable him to pass one test or two; instead, all his knowledge is raised to practice-based fluency, even in handling two or three intertwined hazards at once. Like any good algebraist, he is made to think sometimes in a forward fashion and sometimes in reverse, and so he learns when to concentrate mostly on what he wants to happen and also when to concentrate mostly on avoiding what he does not want to happen. His training time is allocated among subjects so as to minimize damage from his later malfunctions, and so what is most important in his performance gets the most training coverage and is raised to the highest fluency levels. Checklist routines are always mandatory for him. Even after original training, he is forced into a special knowledge maintenance routine: regular use of the aircraft simulator to prevent atrophy through long disuse of skills needed to cope with rare and important problems.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 05 - The Need for More Multidisciplinary Skills (Harvard Law 50th Reunion, 1998-04-24).txt
concept: CHECKLISTS MANDATORY, SIMULATOR MAINTENANCE OBLIGATORY - the six-element pilot system: 'Checklist routines are always mandatory'; skills atrophy without 'regular use of the aircraft simulator'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Operator method (the flags/self-audit ARE checklists; calibration cases ARE the simulator)
evolution_notes: Register P-16 + P-30 (one passage, both claims). Talk 05:49-61. Resolves the claimed tension with the no-formulas rule [E5-43]: checklists are for COVERAGE (never miss a hazard class); formulas are for DECISIONS (and manufacture wanted answers) - the corpus mandates the first and refuses the second. The simulator obligation is the standing re-run discipline: worked calibration cases (Citigroup 2007, Coca-Cola 1988, the MS section 8 table) exist to be re-flown. Talk 11:687-93 companion not re-read this pass.

source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 08 - The Great Financial Scandal of 2003 (written 2000).txt

quote_verbatim: I have what I call an iron prescription that helps me keep sane when I drift toward preferring one intense ideology over another. I feel that I’m not entitled to have an opinion unless I can state the arguments against my position better than the people who are in opposition. I think that I am qualified to speak only when I’ve reached that state.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 10 - USC Gould School of Law Commencement (2007-05-13).txt
concept: THE IRON PRESCRIPTION - 'I'm not entitled to have an opinion unless I can state the arguments against my position better than the people who are in opposition'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Verdict discipline (an IN owes the opposing case); operator rule 9

quote_verbatim: Lollapalooza tendency—the tendency to get extreme consequences from confluences of psychological tendencies acting in favor of a particular outcome This tendency was not in any of the psychology texts I once examined, at least in any coherent fashion, yet it dominates life.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/Talk 11 - The Psychology of Human Misjudgment (PCA revised).txt
concept: LOLLAPALOOZA - extreme consequences from CONFLUENCES of tendencies acting toward one outcome; absent from the textbooks, 'yet it dominates life'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 flags (converging flags are a different event, not a sum); Q2 [E4-36]
evolution_notes: Register P-26. Talk 11:763-765. Flag arithmetic: one fired flag is a prompt to read; several firing TOGETHER toward the same outcome (weak accounting + trumpeted projections + serial issuance + stock-price targeting) are a confluence, and the read must treat them as one reinforcing system - E4-22's cockroach doctrine squared. Same mechanism as E4-36's nonlinear-combination cause of success, running in reverse.

quote_verbatim: Proper allocation of capital is an investor’s number one job. Remember that the highest and best use is always measured by the next best use (opportunity cost). Good ideas are rare—when the odds are greatly in your favor, bet (allocate) heavily.
source_file: Munger Talks (PCA)/99 - End Matter (talk revisits, highlights, index).txt
concept: THE ANALYST'S OWN ALLOCATION - capital allocation is the INVESTOR'S number one job too; highest use measured by next-best use; when odds are greatly favorable, bet heavily
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q5 (the operator audited by the same standard as the CEO); E3-45/E2-62
evolution_notes: Register P-29. PCA End Matter lines 605-609 (the book's distilled investing principles - shelf material, editorial distillation rather than transcribed speech; labelled as such). Closes the loop the MS opens: every test this framework runs on a CEO's allocation (E2-29, E3-58, E3-54) applies to the operator's own portfolio decisions, and the register of runs is the operator's own record.

quote_verbatim: My self-imposed standard limit regarding borrowing is 25% of partnership net worth, although something extraordinary could result in modifying this for a limited period of time.

supports_gate_or_sheet: Q4 leverage (scopes the no-ratio claim: the corpus supplies no COMPANY screen, but does supply the operator's own ceiling); operator discipline
evolution_notes: Register P-13. 1963-01-18 letter lines 252-254; restated 1962-01-24:202 ('standard limit regarding borrowing is 25% of partnership net worth. Oftentimes we owe no money'). Context: the loans 'were to offset work-outs' - hedged, not directional. Corrects v4's absence claim in scope: no leverage ratio exists for judging SUBJECT companies; a number does exist for the analyst's own account, and it is conservative.

quote_verbatim: SAFECO is a much better insurance operation than our own (although we believe certain segments of ours are much better than average), is better than one we could develop and, similarly, is far better than any in which we might negotiate purchase of a controlling interest. Yet our purchase of SAFECO was made at substantially under book value. We paid less than 100 cents on the dollar for the best company in the business, when far more than 100 cents on the dollar is being paid for mediocre companies in corporate transactions. And there is no way to start a new operation - with necessarily uncertain prospects - at less than 100 cents on the dollar. Of course, with a minor interest we do not have the right to direct or even influence management policies of SAFECO. But why should we wish to do this? The record would indicate that they do a better job of managing their operations than we could do ourselves. While there may be less excitement and prestige in sitting back and letting others do the work, we think that is all one loses by accepting a passive participation in excellent management. Because, quite clearly, if one controlled a company run as well as SAFECO, the proper policy also would be to sit back and let management do its job.
concept: PASSIVE PARTICIPATION IN EXCELLENT MANAGEMENT - better than one we could build or buy control of, bought under book; 'sitting back' loses only excitement and prestige
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 (manager quality as a written thesis; the non-control stance chosen, not settled for)
evolution_notes: Register L1-5. 1978 letter lines 426-447 ('We paid less than 100 cents on the dollar for the best company in the business, when far more than 100 cents on the dollar is being paid for mediocre companies in corporate transactions'). The corollary sentence closes it: even WITH control, the proper policy for a SAFECO-quality operation 'would be to sit back and let management do its job.' E4-49's exit-over-engagement doctrine, stated from the happy side.

quote_verbatim: It is important that you understand the magnitude of the errors that have been involved in our reserving. You can thus see for yourselves just how imprecise the process is, and also judge whether we may have some systemic bias that should make you wary of our current and future figures.
concept: THE PUBLISHED SELF-RESTATEMENT - a table of one's own reserving errors, offered so owners can 'judge whether we may have some systemic bias'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 candor (the positive pole; what E2-26 looks like when performed)
evolution_notes: Register L1-25. 1984 letter lines 823-829; the table at 841-855 restates four years of reported underwriting results against corrected figures, and 863-865 names the direction: 'my errors in reporting to you have been substantial and recently have always presented a better underwriting picture than was truly the case.' A filer publishing its own error table WITH direction is the strongest candor evidence the shelf contains; its absence in a reserve-driven filer [E2-50] is the read.

quote_verbatim: You learn a great deal about a person when you purchase a business from him and he then stays on to run it as an employee rather than as an owner. Before the purchase the seller knows the business intimately, whereas you start from scratch. The seller has dozens of opportunities to mislead the buyer - through omissions, ambiguities, and misdirection. After the check has changed hands, subtle (and not so subtle) changes of attitude can occur and implicit understandings can evaporate. As in the courtship-marriage sequence, disappointments are not infrequent. From the time we first met, Gene shot straight 100% of the time - the only behavior pattern he had within him. At the outset of negotiations, he laid all negative factors face up on the table
concept: THE SELLER-STAYS-ON TEST - dozens of opportunities to mislead 'through omissions, ambiguities, and misdirection'; the clean case lays negatives face up
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 (conduct read across an information asymmetry)
evolution_notes: Register L1-33. 1980 letter lines 887-900, the Gene Abegg tribute ('shot straight 100% of the time... for years after the transaction was completed he would tell me periodically of some previously undiscussed items of value'). Public-market form: management's disclosure conduct when THEY hold the information advantage - guidance at issuance, reserve-setting, deal proxies - is the same test.

quote_verbatim: Because we made this choice of unaudited but current figures, as opposed to the alternative of audited but far from current figures, Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. were unable to express an opinion on our 1973 earnings attributable to Blue Chip Stamps.
concept: THE CANDOR-DIRECTION QUALIFIER - Berkshire accepted an auditor's scope disclaimer to report CURRENT reality over stale audited figures; deviation toward candor is not the flag
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 flags (qualifies flag one: judge the DIRECTION of an accounting deviation)
evolution_notes: Register L1-24. 1973 letter line 56. The opposite direction is 1984:925-932 (verified): 'external auditors cannot effectively police... the corpse is supposed to file the death certificate. Under this honor system of mortality, the corpse sometimes gives itself the benefit of the doubt.' A deviation disclosed, reasoned, and against self-interest is candor; one that flatters the filer is the flag.

quote_verbatim: Insurance companies offer standardized policies which can be copied by anyone. Their only products are promises. It is not difficult to be licensed, and rates are an open book. There are no important advantages from trademarks, patents, location, corporate longevity, raw material sources, etc., and very little consumer differentiation to produce insulation from competition. It is commonplace, in corporate annual reports, to stress the difference that people make. Sometimes this is true and sometimes it isn’t. But there is no question that the nature of the insurance business magnifies the effect which individual managers have on company performance.
concept: UNDIFFERENTIATED PRODUCT MAGNIFIES MANAGERS - 'their only products are promises'; no trademark, patent, location or longevity advantage; the manager IS the variance
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 weight rule (the daily-execution determinant's earliest statement, 1977)
evolution_notes: Register L1-6. 1977 letter lines 211-222. Not a fourth weight determinant - the FIRST statement of the one E3-38/E3-43 made canonical: where the product cannot differ, management differences set the outcome, so Q3 weighs more the nearer the business sits to commodity. Completes the arc: 1977 insurance, 1982 the commodity equation [E2-58], 1990 the bank version [E3-29], 1995 retail [E3-38].

quote_verbatim: Our evaluation of the integrity of Mrs. B and her family was demonstrated when we purchased 90% of the business: NFM had never had an audit and we did not request one; we did not take an inventory nor verify the receivables; we did not check property titles. We gave Mrs. B a check for $55 million and she gave us her word. That made for an even exchange.
concept: THE ZERO-VERIFICATION PURCHASE - no audit, no inventory count, no receivables check, no title search: $55 million against her word
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 calibration (the private-deal branch; what a DEMONSTRATED record can license)
evolution_notes: Register L1-11. 1984 letter lines 379-384 ('sell cheap and tell the truth', line 377). Scope, stated: this licenses nothing for public-market runs - the filing remains mandatory [E3-27]. NFM was a control purchase after years of observed conduct in one city; the verification standard scaled with a record the buyer had watched directly. The row exists to mark the branch, not to open it.

quote_verbatim: But when you do receive a communication from us, it will come from the fellow you are paying to run the business. Your Chairman has a firm belief that owners are entitled to hear directly from the CEO as to what is going on and how he evaluates the business, currently and prospectively. You would demand that in a private company; you should expect no less in a public company. A once-a-year report of stewardship should not be turned over to a staff specialist or public relations consultant who is unlikely to be in a position to talk frankly on a manager- to-owner basis.
concept: THE CEO WRITES THE LETTER - 'owners are entitled to hear directly from the CEO'; stewardship reporting is not delegated to specialists or PR consultants
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 candor (authorship as a tell; MS section 5)
evolution_notes: Register L1-34. 1979 letter lines 698-707 ('You would demand that in a private company; you should expect no less in a public company'). Read form: does the shareholder letter engage the business's actual economics and mistakes, or is it a communications product? Pairs with E2-26 (positions-reversed test) and E2-67 (the self-restatement).

quote_verbatim: the managers of the units should be judged by the returns they achieve on the underlying assets; what we pay for a business does not affect the amount of capital its manager has to work with. (If, to become a shareholder and part owner of Commerce Clearing House, you pay, say, six times book value, that does not change CCH's return on equity.)
concept: THE UNDERLYING-ASSETS DENOMINATOR - managers judged on returns on the assets they operate; 'what we pay for a business does not affect the amount of capital its manager has to work with'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q3 primary test (denominator scoping, with E2-43); Q5 [E5-42]
evolution_notes: Register L2-25. 1987 letter lines 77-84 (the CCH six-times-book example). Companions verified: 1985:770-773 ('in some our managers enjoy tailwinds not of their own making, in others they fight unavoidable headwinds') and 1988:115-120 (question three of what reporting must answer: 'How good a job are its managers doing, given the hand they have been dealt?'). Three denominators now scoped: book equity [E2-01], unleveraged net tangible [E2-43], underlying assets ex-purchase-premium [E2-73] - pick by what question is being asked.

quote_verbatim: we had no major common stock investments (that is, over $50 million) other than those we consider permanent or arbitrage holdings. However, Mr. Market will offer us opportunities - you can be sure of that - and, when he does, we will be willing and able to participate. o In the meantime, our major parking place for money is medium-term tax-exempt bonds
concept: THE PARKING PLACE - between opportunities, money waits in permanent holdings, arbitrage and bonds; the box exists so cash pressure never bends the standards
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q5 (the 'or nothing' option has a location); operator discipline
evolution_notes: Register L2-26. 1987 letter lines 1120-1128; companions located: 1985:1332 ('in effect, a parking place for money'), 1986:913. 'Mr. Market will offer us opportunities - you can be sure of that - and, when he does, we will be willing and able to participate.' The ranking's nothing-option [E4-21] is not idleness; it is parked, liquid, and waiting - which is what makes the standards enforceable.

quote_verbatim: what should the measure of an insurer's profitability be? Analysts and managers customarily look to the combined ratio - and it's true that this yardstick usually is a good indicator of where a company ranks in profitability. We believe a better measure, however, to be a comparison of underwriting loss to float developed. This loss/float ratio, like any statistic used in evaluating insurance results, is meaningless over short time periods: Quarterly underwriting figures and even annual ones are too heavily based on estimates to be much good. But when the ratio takes in a period of years, it gives a rough indication of the cost of funds generated by insurance operations. A low cost of funds signifies a good business; a high cost translates into a poor business.

quote_verbatim: Why in the world would a company be assuming 7.5% when it could get nearly 10.5% on government bonds? The answer is that rear-view mirror again: Investors who'd been through the collapse of the Nifty Fifty in the early 1970s were still feeling the pain of the period and were out of date in their thinking about returns. They couldn't make the necessary mental adjustment. Now fast-forward to 2000, when we had long-term governments at 5.4%. And what were the four companies saying in their 2000 annual reports about expectations for their pension funds? They were using assumptions of 9.5% and even 10%. I'm a sporting type, and I would love to make a large bet with the chief financial officer of any one of those four companies, or with their actuaries or auditors, that over the next 15 years they will not average the rates they've postulated. Just look at the math, for one thing. A fund's portfolio is very likely to be one-third bonds, on which--assuming a conservative mix of issues with an appropriate range of maturities--the fund cannot today expect to earn much more than 5%. It's simple to see then that the fund will need to average more than 11% on the two-thirds that's in stocks to earn about 9.5% overall. That's a pretty heroic assumption, particularly given the substantial investment expenses that a typical fund incurs.
source_file: Fortune Essays (Buffett)/2001 - Warren Buffett on the Stock Market.txt
concept: THE PENSION TEST - assumed return read against the OBSERVED bond (7.5% assumed at 10.5% bonds = stale; 9.5% assumed at 5.4% bonds = heroic); restate earnings when heroic

quote_verbatim: There is a third, more subjective, element to an intrinsic value calculation that can be either positive or negative: the efficacy with which retained earnings will be deployed in the future. We, as well as many other businesses, are likely to retain earnings over the next decade that will equal, or even exceed, the capital we presently employ. Some companies will turn these retained dollars into fifty-cent pieces, others into two-dollar bills. This "what-will-they-do-with-the-money" factor must always be evaluated along with the "what-do-we-have-now" calculation in order for us, or anybody, to arrive at a sensible estimate of a company's intrinsic value. That's because an outside investor stands by helplessly as management reinvests his share of the company's earnings. If a CEO can be expected to do this job well, the reinvestment prospects add to the company's current value; if the CEO's talents or motives are suspect, today's value must be discounted. The difference in outcome can be huge. A dollar of then-value in the hands of Sears Roebuck's or Montgomery Ward's CEOs in the late 1960s had a far different destiny than did a dollar entrusted to Sam Walton.

quote_verbatim: Back then, accounting shenanigans of all sorts � many of them ridiculously transparent � were excused or overlooked. Indeed, having an accounting wizard at the helm of an expanding conglomerate was viewed as a huge plus: Shareholders in those instances could be sure that reported earnings would never disappoint, no matter how bad the operating realities of the business might become. In the late 1960s, I attended a meeting at which an acquisitive CEO bragged of his "bold, imaginative accounting." Most of the analysts listening responded with approving nods, seeing themselves as having found a manager whose forecasts were certain to be met, whatever the business results might be. [...] Eventually, however, the clock struck twelve, and everything turned to pumpkins and mice. Once again, it became evident that business models based on the serial issuances of overpriced shares � just like chain-letter models � most assuredly redistribute wealth, but in no way create it. Both phenomena, nevertheless, periodically blossom in our country � they are every promoter's dream � though often they appear in a carefully-crafted disguise. The ending is always the same: Money flows from the gullible to the fraudster. And with stocks, unlike chain letters, the sums hijacked can be staggering. [...] At both BPL and Berkshire, we have never invested in companies that are hell-bent on issuing shares. That behavior is one of the surest indicators of a promotion-minded management, weak accounting, a stock that is overpriced and � all too often � outright dishonesty.

quote_verbatim: And they also know how to use that very valuation to bootstrap value into the business, because if you have a stock that’s selling at 100 that’s worth 10, obviously it’s to your interest to go out and issue a whole lot of shares. And if you do that, when you get all through, the value can be 50. In fact, there’s a lot of chain letter-type stock promotions that are sort of based on the implicit assumption that the management will keep doing that. And if they do it once and build it to 50 by issuing a lot of shares at 100 when it’s worth 10, now the value is 50 and people say, “Well, these guys are so good at that. Let’s pay 200 for it or 300,” and then they could do it again and so on. It’s not usually that — quite that clear in their minds. But that’s the basic principle underlying a lot of stock promotions. And if you get caught up in one of those that is successful, you know, you can run out of money before the promoter runs out of ideas.

And if you do that, when you get all through, the value can be 50'; the market then pays 200 or 300 for the skill and 'they could do it again and so on'; 'if you get caught up in one of those that is successful, you know, you can run out of money before the promoter runs out of ideas'

The row does the arithmetic the other issuance rows assert: an overpriced share is a currency, so issuance at 100 against a value of 10 makes the value 50 and the promotion self-validating for as long as the market pays for the trick. Said while declining to short, which is what makes the last clause a rule about the analyst rather than about the company - 'you can run out of money before the promoter runs out of ideas' is a statement that the thesis and the position can both be right and still lose, and Buffett records in the same answer that the eventual batting average 'is very high'. The corpus's own account of where such stocks come from is in the sentence before: people with very overvalued stocks 'are frequently on some scale between promoter and crook. And that's why they get there.'

quote_verbatim: Some reinsurers � particularly those who, in turn, are accustomed to laying off much of their business on a second layer of reinsurers known as retrocessionaires � are in a weakened condition and would have difficulty surviving a second mega-cat. When a daisy chain of retrocessionaires exists, a single weak link can pose trouble for all. In assessing the soundness of their reinsurance protection, insurers must therefore apply a stress test to all participants in the chain, and must contemplate a catastrophe loss occurring during a very unfavorable economic environment. After all, you only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out. At Berkshire, we retain our risks and depend on no one. And whatever the world's problems, our checks will clear.
concept: THE DAISY CHAIN AND THE STRESS TEST OF EVERY PARTICIPANT - reinsurers 'accustomed to laying off much of their business on a second layer of reinsurers known as retrocessionaires [...] would have difficulty surviving a second mega-cat'; 'When a daisy chain of retrocessionaires exists, a single weak link can pose trouble for all'; insurers 'must therefore apply a stress test to all participants in the chain, and must contemplate a catastrophe loss occurring during a very unfavorable economic environment. After all, you only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out'

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #25. Grepped first: the naked-swimmer sentence was NOT in the ledger, so the passage is cut whole rather than trimmed to the daisy-chain sentences. Two things make it a Q4 instrument and not an aphorism. The correlation is named - the test must assume 'a catastrophe loss occurring during a very unfavorable economic environment', so the counterparty is weakest exactly when it is needed. And the unit of analysis is the chain: 'a single weak link can pose trouble for all', which means a company's own balance sheet is not a sufficient read when its protection is reinsured onward. Berkshire's position is given as the control - 'we retain our risks and depend on no one' - so the row also states what the absence of the shape looks like. Written months after September 11th; E3-78 states the same policy five years earlier.

The word that carries the row is 'respected': the doubt is not about weak counterparties but about sound ones, because the panic and the claim arrive together. quote_verbatim: Those who trade derivatives are usually paid (in whole or part) on "earnings" calculated by mark-to-market accounting. But often there is no real market (think about our contract involving twins) and "mark-to-model" is utilized. This substitution can bring on large-scale mischief. As a general rule, contracts involving multiple reference items and distant settlement dates increase the opportunities for counterparties to use fanciful assumptions. In the twins scenario, for example, the two parties to the contract might well use differing models allowing both to show substantial profits for many years. In extreme cases, mark-to-model degenerates into what I would call mark-to-myth.
concept: MARK-TO-MYTH - 'Those who trade derivatives are usually paid (in whole or part) on "earnings" calculated by mark-to-market accounting. But often there is no real market [...] and "mark-to-model" is utilized'; 'contracts involving multiple reference items and distant settlement dates increase the opportunities for counterparties to use fanciful assumptions'; two parties 'might well use differing models allowing both to show substantial profits for many years'; 'In extreme cases, mark-to-model degenerates into what I would call mark-to-myth'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q4 owner earnings (an earnings figure produced by a model, not a transaction); Q3 honesty (the incentive named: the trader is paid on the model's output); Q4 the named way it dies
evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #26. Grepped first: 'mark-to-myth' was not in the ledger. The row is cited for the phrase but the evidence is the two preceding mechanisms. First the incentive - the mark determines the pay, so the marker is the beneficiary - which is the misjudgment catalogue's own point applied to an accounting policy rather than to a person. Second the arithmetic impossibility that exposes it: both sides of one contract can book profits for years, which cannot both be true and which no single company's statements would reveal. The passage also prices the audit defence honestly: 14,384 contracts and 672 counterparties at General Re Securities, on which 'expert auditors could easily and honestly have widely varying opinions' - so the check a reader would reach for is stated to be incapable, not corrupt.

quote_verbatim: The valuation problem is far from academic: In recent years, some huge-scale frauds and near-frauds have been facilitated by derivatives trades. In the energy and electric utility sectors, for example, companies used derivatives and trading activities to report great "earnings" � until the roof fell in when they actually tried to convert the derivatives-related receivables on their balance sheets into cash. "Mark-to-market" then turned out to be truly "mark-to-myth."
concept: THE SHAPE WITH ITS ENDING ATTACHED, IN A NAMED SECTOR - 'In the energy and electric utility sectors, for example, companies used derivatives and trading activities to report great "earnings" [...] until the roof fell in when they actually tried to convert the derivatives-related receivables on their balance sheets into cash. "Mark-to-market" then turned out to be truly "mark-to-myth"'

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #26. The companion to E4-68 eleven lines later, and the more usable of the two because it names the moment of discovery and the test that discovers it: the attempt to convert the derivatives-related receivable into cash. That is Q4's cash question asked of a balance-sheet asset rather than of an earnings line, and it is the reason the framework's owner-earnings figure starts from cash and not from a mark. The passage closes with the asymmetry, which belongs to Q3: 'the marking errors in the derivatives business have not been symmetrical. Almost invariably, they have favored either the trader who was eyeing a multi-million dollar bonus or the CEO who wanted to report impressive "earnings"'; and 'Only much later did shareholders learn that the reported earnings were a sham.'

quote_verbatim: Through our Clayton purchase, we acquired a significant manufactured-housing finance operation. Clayton, like others in this business, had traditionally securitized the loans it originated. The practice relieved stress on Clayton's balance sheet, but a by-product was the "front-ending" of income (a result dictated by GAAP). We are in no hurry to record income, have enormous balance-sheet strength, and believe that over the long-term the economics of holding our consumer paper are superior to what we can now realize through securitization. So Clayton has begun to retain its loans.
concept: THE FRONT-ENDING OF INCOME NAMED, AND THE REMEDY CHOSEN AGAINST IT - securitisation 'relieved stress on Clayton's balance sheet, but a by-product was the "front-ending" of income (a result dictated by GAAP)'; 'We are in no hurry to record income, have enormous balance-sheet strength, and believe that over the long-term the economics of holding our consumer paper are superior to what we can now realize through securitization. So Clayton has begun to retain its loans'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q4 owner earnings (income recognised at origination rather than earned over the loan's life); Q3 rationality (a management choosing later income over sooner); Q4 the named way it dies
evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #26. The cleanest statement in the corpus that a reporting convention, not a fraud, can put the profit of a multi-year loan into the year it is written - 'a result dictated by GAAP' - and it is stated as a by-product of a financing decision rather than as an accusation. Two uses. It names the question to ask of any originate-and-distribute lender: is the reported income the spread earned or the gain booked at sale? And it records the corpus acting on its own answer at a cost, because retaining the loans defers the income and consumes balance sheet: 'We are in no hurry to record income.' Berkshire's stated funding rule for the retained book is in the same passage - finance interest-bearing receivables 'almost entirely with debt (just as a bank would)' - which is the shape's antidote, not a contradiction of the conservatism.

And it’s another case where the accounting profession has failed the wider civilization.

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #26. A year before the 2002 letter's derivatives section, and it goes further than E4-68 and E4-69 in one respect that matters to a reader deciding how much weight an audit opinion carries: the charge is against the standard and its setters, not against the individual company - 'the accounting profession sold out' - so a clean opinion on a front-ended income statement is consistent with Munger's claim rather than evidence against it. The chain of causation is given in full and is four links long: compensation is calculated on the reported figure, the figure is set by a model, the model's optimism is what the field wants, and the profession accommodated it. Buffett adds the measurement in the next answer: single positions at Salomon 'mismarked by close to $20 million'.

quote_verbatim: Historically, the survival of a local electric company did not depend on its efficiency. In fact, a "sloppy" operation could do just fine financially. That's because utilities were usually the sole supplier of a needed product and were allowed to price at a level that gave them a prescribed return upon the capital they employed. The joke in the industry was that a utility was the only business that would automatically earn more money by redecorating the boss's office. And some CEOs ran things accordingly. That's all changing. Today, society has decided that federally-subsidized wind and solar generation is in our country's long-term interest. Federal tax credits are used to implement this policy, support that makes renewables price-competitive in certain geographies. Those tax credits, or other government-mandated help for renewables, may eventually erode the economics of the incumbent utility, particularly if it is a high-cost operator.
