In fact, a "sloppy" operation could do just fine financially'; utilities 'were allowed to price at a level that gave them a prescribed return upon the capital they employed. The joke in the industry was that a utility was the only business that would automatically earn more money by redecorating the boss's office. And some CEOs ran things accordingly'; 'Those tax credits, or other government-mandated help for renewables, may eventually erode the economics of the incumbent utility, particularly if it is a high-cost operator'

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #14. Cut as ONE row rather than two, on E3-76's precedent: the regulated return, the redecorating joke and the subsidised entrant are one argument, and splitting them would let the joke be cited as colour or the erosion be cited as a policy risk, when the corpus's point is that the first CAUSES the second - a cost base assembled under a prescribed return is what a subsidised competitor erodes. Three things to keep with it. The hedge is Buffett's: 'may eventually erode', and the condition is named - 'particularly if it is a high-cost operator'. The policy is not opposed; it is described as something 'society has decided'. And the row is written about a business Berkshire owns, with the claimed defence being the thing the shape attacks: BHE's 'long-established emphasis on efficiency [...] even when the company didn't need it to attain authorized earnings', evidenced in the same section by 3,700 people producing 19 million megawatt-hours before 1999 against 3,500 producing 29 million after.

Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn't have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent. The consequence has been huge numbers of repossessions and pitifully low recoveries on the units repossessed.

When "securitization" then became popular in the 1990s, further distancing the supplier of funds from the lending transaction, the industry's conduct went from bad to worse. Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn't have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent'

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #18. First of two rows on the manufactured-housing passage; E4-73 is lines 282-289, the model required instead. The distinction this row draws is the one a run needs at Q1: the product was fine and improving - the industry 'can deliver very good value to home purchasers' and 'both the quality and variety of manufactured houses consistently improved' - and the failure was entirely in distribution and financing. So a product verdict is not a business verdict. Securitisation is named as the accelerant and the reason is given as distance, 'further distancing the supplier of funds from the lending transaction', which is a structural test a reader can apply rather than a judgment about anyone's character. The corpus prices its own error in the same section: Buffett bought Oakwood debt and 'Oakwood rather promptly went bankrupt'.

quote_verbatim: Today, the manufactured housing industry remains awash in problems. Delinquencies continue high, repossessed units still abound and the number of retailers has been halved. A different business model is required, one that eliminates the ability of the retailer and salesman to pocket substantial money up front by making sales financed by loans that are destined to default. Such transactions cause hardship to both buyer and lender and lead to a flood of repossessions that then undercut the sale of new units. Under a proper model � one requiring significant down payments and shorter-term loans � the industry will likely remain much smaller than it was in the 90s. But it will deliver to home buyers an asset in which they will have equity, rather than disappointment, upon resale.

But it will deliver to home buyers an asset in which they will have equity, rather than disappointment, upon resale'

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #18. Second of two rows; E4-72 is lines 256-262, the model being described. This is the operative half, because it converts the diagnosis into something checkable at Q1: can the person making the sale be paid in full before the loan can go bad? Where the answer is yes, the volume is not demand. Two features of the row are worth keeping. It names the terms that fix it - significant down payments, shorter-term loans - so the test has a positive form and not only a negative one. And it states the price of the fix without hedging: the industry 'will likely remain much smaller', which is the corpus declining to promise that the sound model is also the larger one. Written in the year Berkshire bought Clayton, whose conduct the same section grades as 'considerably better than its major competitors' rather than clean.

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #13. Small in the letter and precise in what it shows: a fifteen-year-old, profitable unit of one of the corpus's own franchise businesses was set for closure because the counterparty holding a non-owned input asked for the whole of the profit - 'would have wiped out the store's profit' - and See's was ready to close rather than pay. The bargaining outcome is in the corpus too, and a run must not cite the row without it: 263 customers wrote and telephoned, a newspaper picked up the story, and 'our landlord offered us a satisfactory deal'. quote_verbatim: The question is about the future of the tobacco business? I don’t — I probably know no more about that then you do because it’s fraught with questions that relate to societal attitudes and you can form an opinion on that just as well as I could. But, I would not like to have a significant percentage of my net worth in the tobacco business myself, but — They may have better futures than I envision. I don’t really think that I have special insights on that. [...] You have to come to a conclusion as to how society is going to want to treat — and the present administration for that matter. And the economics of the business may be fine, but that doesn’t mean it has a great future.
concept: GOOD ECONOMICS IS NOT A FUTURE - 'the economics of the business may be fine, but that doesn't mean it has a great future'; the reason given is that the question is 'fraught with questions that relate to societal attitudes' on which 'you can form an opinion on that just as well as I could'; and the personal conclusion: 'I would not like to have a significant percentage of my net worth in the tobacco business myself'
supports_gate_or_sheet: Q4 the named way it dies (society, not a competitor); verdict machinery (UNKNOWABLE: no document resolves a societal attitude); Q2 franchise (an intact moat with no claim on the future)
evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #22. The ordering brief cited line 427 for the sentence; on disk the sentence is at line 431, in Buffett's follow-up, so the row is cut as two fragments in document order, 427 and 431, and the line locator records both. This is the sharpest separation in the corpus between the two things Q2 and Q4 ask: the economics can be excellent and the future still unavailable, and the corpus does not resolve the tension by pretending to a view - 'I probably know no more about that then you do' ('then' is in the transcript; kept per PRIME RULE 1). What it does instead is the verdict machinery working: the input is a societal attitude, no document would settle it, so it closes as unknowable and the position is declined. Munger's whole answer at the end of the exchange is one word: 'No.'

Five years after E3-80 and the same verdict, now with the channel named: legislative rather than diffuse societal attitude. The row's value is the conjunction, because the two halves are what the framework's UNKNOWABLE verdict is made of - a serious threat, and no method of estimating it - and Munger states them together without resolving either into a discount rate or a haircut. Buffett's answer immediately after supplies the comparison that keeps this from being generic political risk: 'there's no comparison between the threat to tobacco, currently, with the threat to pharmaceuticals in 1993', and the distinction he draws is that with pharmaceuticals 'Nobody was against pharmaceuticals', the dispute being about pricing and distribution, whereas 'tobacco's a different story'. So the corpus does grade this class of risk; it just will not price this instance.

quote_verbatim: There have been plenty of mergers, non-dilutive in this limited sense, that were instantly value destroying for the acquirer. We believe calculation of dilution from this viewpoint to be all-important (and too seldom made).

And some mergers that have diluted current and near-term earnings per share have in fact been value-enhancing. What really counts is whether a merger is dilutive or anti-dilutive in terms of intrinsic business value (a judgment involving consideration of many variables). We believe calculation of dilution from this viewpoint to be all-important (and too seldom made)'

evolution_notes: Added 2026-09-20 from the corpus ruling on survival shapes; grounds shape #24. The row is the corpus separating the accounting test from the economic one, in both directions: a merger can pass the earnings-per-share screen and destroy value instantly, and it can fail that screen and create value. The sentence before is where the earnings test is put in its place - 'current earnings per share (or even earnings per share of the next few years) are an important variable in most business valuations, but far from all powerful' - and the parenthetical at the end is the finding a reader should carry to any acquirer's record: the calculation that matters is 'too seldom made', so its absence is the base case and not a red flag on its own. 1982 is also where the letter's next paragraph refuses the language of the transaction, since 'B Sells to A' hides which party is paying.
